inline.s: Wu Zhan of the Qing dynasty was a county clerk. His dwelling stood beside the Jing Stream. The stream had a spring, exceedingly clear, and all the clerks relied upon it. Wu Zhan built a fence to shield and protect it, so that no filth might enter. One day, beside the spring, he found a white snail and put it in a jar. Each time he came home from outside, food and drink in the kitchen were already prepared. His heart was greatly astonished. One day he secretly peeped in: it was a woman, who came forth from the snail and worked with her own hands. Wu Zhan hurried toward her; the woman, greatly flustered, had no time to return into the shell, and told him the truth, saying: I am the spirit of the spring. The Most High, because you reverently protected the source of the spring, and knowing that you dwelt as a widower, commanded me to prepare your meals. If you eat my meals, you shall attain the Way. With these words she vanished.

Han Yin Zifang was a man of the utmost filial piety, and had a benevolent and kindly heart as well. It happened that on the winter sacrifice day, while the morning meal was being cooked, the Kitchen God suddenly appeared before him. Zifang bowed twice, and thereafter, whenever the winter sacrifice day came round, he offered sacrifice to him. From this he grew very rich, equal to a lord of the land. In time his grandson Yin Shi had a daughter who became empress, and the family obtained a fief as marquises. For this reason the descendants of the Yin clan sacrificed to the hearth god generation after generation.
Xiang Lin was by nature half mad. One day, sitting on the plank roof north of the hearth, he dreamed that the Lord of the Hearth rebuked him, and his family was ruined and scattered at once.
Food is the resource by which life is nourished. Man is one of the Three Powers; how can he make light of it? If one leaps over it, it is in every case a sin. How can one fail to take warning?

In the Tang dynasty an official went into the mountains until he reached a lonely, inaccessible place, where he saw a wineshop. He bought wine and drank it. A woman first took his money and went inside; after a long while she came out carrying wine, whose color was like blood, and which tasted very sweet. He wished to drink again, and the woman, weeping, told him: I am no living person. Because in my life I was extravagant without measure, drinking wine without restraint, and would often tread underfoot leftover soup and scraps of meat and then give them to others to eat, I have received this retribution. Whenever someone buys wine, I must draw out the blood of my own body to supply it. The official, greatly frightened, turned back. How could there be a wineshop on a high mountain? One may suppose that this official had always been careless about food and drink, and that the underworld borrowed this to warn and reform him.

Zhai Lin of the Song dynasty once escorted Master Zhengshu on his westward journey. On the road they lodged at a monastery. The place where he sat happened to have its back to a holy image. The master said: Turn your chair; do not sit with your back to it. Lin said: Is it not that we should reverence it because his disciples revere him? The master said: Whenever a thing bears human form and countenance, one should not treat it with disrespect. Guishan heard of this and greatly admired his words, saying with delight: If one does not presume to slight even that which resembles a man, then how much more toward a man himself! This shows it plainly. If to turn one's back is already not permitted, how much less to leap over it?

The human body is supremely precious, and to obtain a human body is supremely difficult. The Buddha said that when a person is about to be born, the Minister of the Nine Heavens is in the court, the Nine Heavens offer congratulations, Taiyi holds the tally, the Lord Emperor ranks the destiny, the Master of Registers inscribes the record, the Master of Destinies fixes the reckoning, the Five Emperors oversee the birth, the Holy Mother guards the chamber, and the gods of heaven and the spirits of earth of the three realms all stand watch. To be restored to the human path, to be lifted into the form of the Great Yang — it alarms heaven and startles earth; its preciousness cannot be spoken of. What fault had you to repay, that you dared kill it? A woman who runs off in lust, conceives, and then procures abortion is worse than a beast; there is no reasoning with her. There are even those who, being poor, grow weary of many children; or who destroy the child once it is born; or who procure abortion before it is born. The karma of killing man cannot be repented or redeemed. The lives of creatures are most minute, and yet men still wish to set them free and keep the precept against killing — how much more for sons and daughters? That men in this one life have no son, or bear a child that does not live, or in old age see their sons die before them — all this is the retribution drawn down by having made such evil karma in former lives.

Qian Bangwei, magistrate of Guixi, found that by the custom of the place, when a daughter was born she was very often not raised. He therefore set forth for the people the right rule of conduct, and strictly enforced reward and punishment: whoever killed a daughter, five households should be punished together for it. By this means those who were kept alive could not be numbered. Bangwei afterward became prefect of Tingzhou, enjoyed a great age, and his sons and grandsons all flourished. Now for forbidding the destroying of the unborn and the casting away of the born, he obtained such a recompense as this. Men of today ought at every turn to exhort and instruct the people: the merit of it is no small thing.

Guo Yin had a daughter named Yinfeng. She was seized and dragged away by two ghosts, and made to pass through all eighteen hells. In the last hell, a king sat upon the throne in the hall, and below him were ranged several hundred women, each with a small child that clung to her legs, wailing and demanding its life. Some had drowned their daughters because they had borne too many; some, being poor, had not raised the child once it was born; some, when a wife grew jealous that a concubine had borne a son, had beaten the child to death in the womb; some had poisoned a child conceived in secret; some had injured it in a quarrel; some had beaten and flung it until it died because they were angered by its crying; some, through careless watching, had let the child die before its time. The king questioned them one by one, and not one of them was without shackles on her body; they were withered and thin, and piteous to see. When Yinfeng had returned, she told her father all of it, and he therefore wrote a great inscription on the wall of Tianning Monastery as a warning.

The woman Yang Asheng had been poor and sickly from childhood, and in her later years was in still worse straits. As she was dying she spoke to herself, saying: In a former life I was a physician. I failed in careful examination. A woman said she was ill with a worm in her belly, and I could not distinguish that she was with child. I hastily gave her yuanhua wine to bring it away, and the woman died together with the two children in her womb. Thus by one act I killed three people. The officers of the underworld held me guilty, and when my suffering was complete, I was punished with the body of a woman. Now it is already the third time, and life after life I am forever a base slave, long bound in hunger and thirst, often sick and seldom at ease. You may tell the physicians of the world to take me for a warning. With these words she died.

Emperor Wen said: When a man's son is unfilial, there are in truth the statutes of Heaven by which he is put to death. But to kill a child that has done no wrong is to kill the people of the whole world. And if a man wishes to kill a child, why does he not restrain his desire? Yet he dares to kill a man and give it no thought. In this present age, how can one be sure that such people do not exist? I have seen those who suffer punishment in Fengdu, and very many of them have committed this offense. Let all men quickly awake and repent; do not hasten the chastisement of Heaven.
He Longtu's Song of Warning Against Drowning Daughters says:
The tiger and the wolf are fiercest in nature, yet still they know that there are father and son.
Man is the soul of all the myriad things; how is he then less than these?
Whether a son is born or a daughter, held at the breast they are but one and the same.
I hear that when a daughter is killed, the pain of it is past compare.
The afterbirth blood is still running down; her mouth has no words to speak.
She wails in the water of the basin, and only after a long while comes to die.
Alas, how can a parent's heart be cruel to such a degree?
Therefore I exhort our people: never kill your daughters.
A thornwood pin and a hempen skirt will hardly make you poor.
A woman's nature is softest and most kind; she loves her kin more than her sons.
A son is often away from home; a daughter stays beside her parents.
A son is often stubborn and cross; a daughter is ever obedient to her parents.
A son is often far abroad; a daughter stays near her parents.
A son has little grief; a daughter weeps for her parents.
A daughter has a heart of filial love, and again and again she saves her parents.
When a daughter finds a worthy husband, again and again she brings her parents honor.
Do you not see Tiying, that girl, who freed her father from the pain of mutilation?
Do you not see Tang Xiang, that girl, who saved her father by seizing the tiger?
Qin, at the age of eighteen, brought her father's body home for burial.
Cao E, at the age of fourteen, dived into the river to find her father's corpse.
Shuxian grieved that her father drowned, and clasped the corpse and floated on the water.
Yuan's daughter, whose mother was palsied, when the fire came could not rise.
The girl wept and could not bear to flee; she chose to burn to death with her mother.
A Song girl was known as Chen San; her parents were poor as washed-out rags.
The three sisters shared their gruel, living wholly on water chestnut gleanings.
When her parents died she would not marry, but kept their grave until her teeth fell out.
A Tang girl, Yu Hezi, whose father and brother both fell in war.
Hezi was just seventeen; barefoot she walked to the far frontier.
A beggar, she carried the bones home, and paid for the burial by her weaving.
She cut her hair and marred her face, and then kept watch at the grave.
Her great fidelity reached the emperor's ear; a decree proclaimed her gate.
Filial indeed was the lady of the Xiao house; her parents died in a foreign land.
The lady was but sixteen years old, and she bore the coffin home to her village.
The boatman cheated her in her loneliness, and abandoned the coffin on the way.
She gathered earth with her hands and heaped a tomb, the lady with only one maid beside her.
She marred her face and mourned day and night, and built her hut by the waterside.
When the mourning was full she would not put it off; when suitors came she would not wed.
Whoever could bring back the coffin, to him alone she would give herself.
And indeed she married the man who brought the coffin back, an old lieutenant of Yangshe.
The daughter of the Tu family of Dongwu; her father was blind and crippled with palsy.
The house had no grain for the next night's meal; kin and neighbors all cast them off.
The girl then moved her two parents far away to a hempen hut.
By day she gathered wood and traded for grain; by night she spun hemp and traded for wadding.
Her two parents at last fulfilled their years; she carried earth and made their grave.
She kept the grave and never married, only because she had no brother.
Of the wise and filial women of old, how many there are, past all recording.
Some were given gold by the officers; some were honored with imperial gifts.
Some became consorts of princes; some became the wives of lords.
If a man can keep another's life alive, the recompense should not go astray.
I exhort the people of the world: better return to the Way of Heaven.
Do not say an infant girl is foolish, and does not know to resent and repay.
If a daughter's life her own kin will not pity, how can they be sure to pity their own lives?
No heir, and years cut short: fearful is the law of the underworld.
And when the day comes to demand a life, it is too late to gnaw one's navel in regret.
Why not keep her whole and living, so that both bone and flesh win blessing?

Hidden and secret — this is not one thing only. Such matters as lewdness, theft, and licentiousness, and all that cannot be known by Heaven or spoken before men, are of this kind. But the greatest of them must belong to the deeds of lust. This is why the Most High wrote this passage after the injuring of children and the procuring of abortion. Surely there is a reason for it.

Mao Qizong said: North of the town of Fuliang there lived Zhang Mingsan, who followed his father to official post in Qiongya. The government quarters adjoined the residence of Commander Li. Li had two daughters, both beautiful, and Mingsan carried on illicit relations with them. When he returned home he secretly took the two girls along in his boat, intending to cross the sea. Li pursued him in hot haste; at his wits' end, Mingsan shoved both girls into the water. Ten years later Mingsan fell ill with lumbago and engaged a physician named Sun to treat him. The medicine brought slight relief, but that night Sun dreamed he was fishing at the Mei in his village, and in the seawater stood two women, naked, who seized his robe and said: "We are from Qiong. We came to cure Zhang of his sickness. Will you really rob us of our merit?" With that they dragged Sun into the water. He woke in a cold sweat that soaked his back. At dawn he told what he had seen, and Mingsan, beating his breast, sighed: "My karma has caught up with me. I am as good as dead." Indeed he died within the month. Here is a case of a man and women whose deeds were deeply hidden, and who each in turn received their retribution. Mingsan and the two girls first met in secret and then fled in secret; the girls in the end died by Mingsan's hand, and Mingsan in the end died by the spirits of the two girls. One may call this retribution most cunning and yet never leaking. On the whole, to violate another man's wife or daughter and to wreck another man's official career are the two things most often done in hiding and most destructive of the human heart and of Heaven's principle. Therefore he who violates the wives and daughters of others will have his own wife and daughter violated, and he who wrecks the career of others will have his own career wrecked. As the saying goes: In a dark room the heart may fail, but the divine eye is as lightning. How can one not take heed?

Hui means the last day of the month, when the Director of Fate and the Kitchen God memorialize the merits and faults of the world's people. La means the five la days, when the Heavenly Lords of the five qi assemble to reckon the good and evil of the living. On those days the Heavenly Lords hold audience at the Mystic Capital and govern the human world, the underworld, the Five Peaks, and the thirty-six thousand spirits of yin and yang; they determine each person's good and evil, guilt and blessing, honor, emolument, and allotted years, and all matters of fortune and misfortune, life and death, entering each one in the registers. The first day of the first month is called the Heaven La; the fifth day of the fifth month, the Earth La; the seventh day of the seventh month, the La of the Way and Its Virtue; the first day of the tenth month, the Year La; the eighth day of the twelfth month, the Prince La. Whoever meets such a day and has committed even one fault has it written in the black register — can he atone for his guilt? Moreover, on these days the Northern Emperor of Fengdu and the Heavenly Lord of the Great Yin bring forth the long-departed ancestors, parents, and kin of the living, and even the ghost souls in the dark prisons, and question them: how many years have they dwelt in the realm of darkness, what piled-up crimes and tangled feuds brought them to this pass, where now stand their graves, and who are their descendants by name? Once the names of descendants, brothers, kin, and the nine clans are obtained, they are gathered and assessed, and these become the record of the living person's guilt. If through piled-up kalpas no one has offered deliverance, the burden is surely extended to the living. Moreover on these days the spirits of the departed kin are all released and each returns to the family home to receive offerings. As descendants, one ought to rely on the methods of the Way to sacrifice and to ransom them. To give oneself over to singing and dancing is to offend Heaven, Earth, and the ancestors. On the hui and la days, then, should one offer deliverance, or should one sing and dance?

Huaiyin's Qiang Fu was careful in conduct all his life and modest and gentle in his dealings. On the first and fifteenth of each month and on the la days he read and recited the Sanskrit scriptures and bowed in worship to the spirits, never slackening from first to last. It happened that on the New Year's Day, the Heaven La, a petty fellow got drunk and reviled him. Fu shut his door and paid no heed. His family and neighbors could not bear it, but Fu said: "On a festival like this, who does not drink? To run wild after wine is common human weakness. If I were to contend with him, would I not be very small-minded?" At that single word the spirits above were moved. That night, as he dozed, he dreamed he came to a certain place and saw a man in a golden crown and purple robe, who said to him: "You could bear on the Heaven La what others cannot bear. The Most High commends you. I grant you blessing and long life; your sons and grandsons shall wear cap and sash for generations." Suddenly he was awakened by someone calling. In the end he lived past eighty; two sons and a grandson all passed the examinations on the classics, and down to the great-great-grandsons the family has continued to flourish in the schools without break. This is one who examined himself on the hui and la days. Those who on such days shout wildly, sing and dance, and give themselves to wine and license violate the precepts of Heaven's truth and must lose the heart of self-cultivation; truly they wear away their blessings and emoluments and cut short their allotted years. Take heed, take heed.

What a month accomplishes rests on its first day; what a day accomplishes rests on its dawn. At such a time one should calm the mind and be pure and still, so as to accord with the truth of the Way. If one gives a single shout of anger, turbid qi rises with the liver and true qi scatters with the sound; then the spirit grows dim and the qi turbid, and good thoughts are extinguished. An old poem says: All the afflictions that beset the mind all spring from not forbearing; facing the moment as before a mirror, the wonder lies in the light. The Buddha's word bids us seek non-contention; the Confucian books prize not striving; a fine and happy road it is, yet few in the world walk it. The Buddhist scriptures say: Anger is the root of losing all good dharmas and the cause of falling into evil paths; one should cast it off at once and not let it grow. Thus a shout of anger burdens a person greatly. One should be careful even on ordinary days — how much more at the dawn of the month.

Chen Ying's wife, née Zhao, was fierce by nature and fond of quarreling; on the first of the month she was worse than ever. Those who came and went from her house heard nothing but unending shouts of rage and curses. Suddenly a Daoist arrived. "What do you want?" she asked. "I sell a spirit elixir," he said. "Take it and you will live long." Delighted, she bought and swallowed it — and was struck dumb.

The Han Minister of Works Diwu Lun had an aged mother who could not come to his post, and whenever the hui, la, first, or fifteenth days came round he grieved and wept with longing, bowing to Heaven and praying for her years. Alas, how the noble men of old felt the season and cherished their parents. And those who sing and dance and shout in anger — what are they about? How much less will they reflect, when what was said above about pursuing the distant dead and delivering the departed is set out in such detail.

The north is where the Lord of the Northern Dipper dwells; the North Pole is the pivot of Heaven. The three realms and ten directions, the myriad spirits and all the perfected, are all subject to it. Thus the Dipper's pole in mid-heaven is called the Most Honored, and how could the place where the Honored One dwells be touched with filth? According to the rites, a son or daughter-in-law may not hiccup, sneeze, spit, or blow the nose beside father or mother, father-in-law or mother-in-law, because it is disrespectful. How much less may one spit or even urinate toward the north, which is the direction of the spirits, when spittle itself is not allowed.

There was a man in the Wu region who rose at night and urinated naked toward the north. Suddenly he saw a black banner blot out the sky and the Perfected Warrior appear in person. He crawled on hands and knees into the house and lay ill for months, only recovering after repentance. The Scripture of Long Life says: east in spring, south in summer, west in autumn, north in winter — whichever direction the monthly indicator points, to offend there is to offend the handle of the Northern Dipper, and the shortening of one's years is swiftest of all. From this we see that every direction has its prohibition, not the due north alone.

The Qian family of Changshu was a great clan. In the Zhengde era a great fire spread and burned for three nights before it stopped. Amid the ashes a small three-bay tower alone survived — it belonged to the Qian family's fourth branch, where a widow and her daughter-in-law lived in seclusion together above. When the fire was blazing on all four sides and the two had no way to escape, they remembered that they had always served the Dipper spirit and could only knock their heads and beg for rescue. Suddenly they saw seven men in vermilion robes standing beneath the eaves, raising their sleeves and waving the fire away, and it scattered at their gesture. Thus the widow and her daughter-in-law came to no harm, while on all four sides not a single rafter remained. The whole region was moved and converted, and all honored the Northern Dipper. Cases of those who revered the Northern Dipper and obtained lengthened life, relief from sickness, preservation of life, escape from disaster, granted blessings, and continuing posterity, so that water and fire, bandits and thieves, demons and monsters, pestilence and plague did not touch them — such cases are too many to count. Here one is given as an example of the rest. Yet the essential point is that one must do good before one can move Heaven. If a man can do so, how could he spit or urinate toward the north?

The Yellow Emperor's Kitchen Scripture says: at the stove one must not sing or weep, curse or shout. Chanting and weeping, grief and joy, differ from one another, yet all alike are disrespectful to the spirit and will surely cut short one's emolument and years. Moreover, people today do not dare to raise their voices or speak wildly before a magistrate's court; how is it that before the spirits they have no scruples at all? Foolish men and foolish women should most strictly take heed. That reverence or irreverence brings fortune or calamity has been made clear above.

According to the regulations of the Celestial Master's school, the ash and fire beneath the stove are called the dung of the crouching dragon, and therefore one must not burn incense with them. I have myself read through the teachings, and the taboos concerning incense and fire do not stop at this one matter. For instance, one must not burn paper with a wick soaked in oil; this is called vainly piling up wax money, which accumulates on the Eastern Peak like a mountain and is accepted neither by the bureaus of Heaven and Earth nor by those of yin and yang. Again, when making offerings to the Perfected Warrior, one must not use plums in summer or pomegranates in winter. When invoking a Perfected One to descend, one must not burn nipple incense; sandalwood is called bathing incense, the monthly rose is called an out-of-season flower, and the golden paulownia is called a ghost flower. All these should be avoided. To avoid them not, and so bring offense upon oneself — how much better to revere and follow the teaching?

The Essential Collection of Sutras says: to awaken to principle through events, one must rely on forms to guide one to the truth; to gaze upon the holy countenance, one depends on flowers and incense for the offering. The Buddha said that after the Tathagata's nirvana, if there be anyone who with a single flower or a single stick of incense makes an offering, who with a single handful of water removes impurity, who takes a single step toward the buddhas and once calls on the name of the Buddha, such a person cannot possibly fall into the three evil paths. The Commentary on the Vimalakirti Sutra says: incense is the name for freedom from defilement, and it has the power to spread fragrance and diffuse sweetness on high. The Record of Responsive Communion says: the stench of the human world rises into the sky for four hundred thousand li, and the pure heavens find it all loathsome. Yet because they have received the Buddha's charge to protect the Dharma, and the Buddha himself still dwells among men, the heavenly hosts dare not fail to come. Therefore in the Buddha Dharma incense is the foremost of offerings. The Avatamsaka Sutra says: in the Heaven of Good Dharma there is an incense called Pure Adornment; if one burns a single pellet and perfumes the air with it, it causes all the heavens to turn their minds to the Buddha. Since this is so, how can one fail to take heed against burning incense at the stove?

Zhou Kaishan of the Song dynasty recited the Avatamsaka Sutra, and there was another monk who could recite the Diamond Sutra. Both died suddenly at the same time. King Yama invited Kaishan to recite the sutra and treated him with great reverence. He then asked the other monk to recite the Diamond Sutra, but his own heart was not very reverent. When the recitation was done, the King said: both monks, by the merit of reciting sutras, have their years extended by two cycles of twelve; he who holds the Avatamsaka should be held in still greater reverence, and one day he will no longer come to my court. Then the Diamond-reciting monk was overcome with shame. He asked where Kaishan lived, wishing to visit him. When he awoke he went straight to Luzhou, found Kaishan, and questioned him. Kaishan said: whenever I recite, I first purify my clothes, sprinkle and sweep a clean room with perfumed water, and only then take fire from flint, or drill wood for fire, to burn incense; I make my vows with a solemn mind, and open my mouth as though face to face with the Buddha. I have never dared be remiss. Had I no such pure fire, I would never dare lightly use any other fire to burn incense. The Diamond-reciting monk thanked him, saying: I have been at fault. Whenever I recite I use fire from the stove to burn incense. In this one matter alone my irreverence is great. Now the burning of incense is meant to express a reverent heart; it must be clean and pure before it may be burned. If by chance the stove holds filthy fuel and one uses it to burn incense, then the reverent heart becomes a profane one instead. Therefore the Most High warns against it.

Though firewood lies below the stove, its qi in truth rises; if the fuel is filthy and impure, its foul and turbid qi offends the Kitchen God — this is the first reason not to use it. Since it has been used to cook food, one cannot avoid using it for offerings as well — this is the second reason. Its smoke rises into the void, and the spirits are easily angered — this is the third reason. Those who cook should most strictly take heed.

In the seventh year of the Zhenghe era of the Song, Li Ba had suffered from leprosy for three years, and a hundred medicines had done him no good. Before Li fell ill he had recited the sutra of Great Compassion Avalokitesvara through three full collections. One day a monk suddenly came and gave him a single pill, telling him to take it. Li kept it carelessly and would not swallow it at once. That night he dreamed that the monk who had given the medicine said: I am Avalokitesvara. Because you habitually used filthy firewood for steaming and cooking, you offended the ghosts and spirits, and so contracted this leprosy. And because you once recited the sutras through three collections, I have specially given you one pill of the Elixir of Relief from Suffering. Why have you not taken it? When he woke he took it at once. Within seven days the skin of his whole body peeled away and his beard and eyebrows grew again. Filthy firewood offends the spirits, and one should indeed take heed of it. As for using the branches and trunks of peach and willow as firewood for cooking, this too offends the Kitchen God, and the Daoist scriptures warn against it. One should know this as well.

The upright and noble man fears other men in the light and fears the spirits in the dark; therefore even in a dark room or a leaking house he is as solemn as if the spirits were face to face with him. Moreover, the spirits dwell in the dark and are present everywhere; and night belongs to yin, the very time when the hundred spirits meet and peer about. How can one fail to be careful, and so bring down misfortune on oneself?

In Pengcheng there was a girl of an official family. Less than a month after her marriage she raved without cause, ran about naked, and knew no shame at all. Doctors and prayers could not cure her. It happened that Master Zhang the Perfected One was returning to the capital, and the household head submitted a petition to him. The Perfected One sent a disciple to cure her with talismans, but he retreated in confusion while the girl raved and stripped herself as before. Then the Perfected One went in person to perform the rites and summoned a general, who appeared in form below the altar. Just as the Dark Emperor arrived, the girl's expression changed and she said: a mere common woman, naked in the middle of the night, offending my heavenly spirits — she deserved open execution; but since the trouble was taken to bring a Perfected One here, she is pardoned. With that she fell headlong to the ground, and her illness was cured.

The Beginning of Spring, the Spring Equinox, the Beginning of Summer, the Summer Solstice, the Beginning of Autumn, the Autumn Equinox, the Beginning of Winter, and the Winter Solstice are the eight nodes. On these days the heavenly spirits and perfected ones go forth in their divisions to spread transformation universally and to teach and deliver the multitudes, recording guilt and blessing in detail. People should be pure, still, and harmonious, recollecting and examining themselves, advancing in good and dismissing evil, entering the right and leaving the crooked, so as to match the heart of the Most High and the assembled Perfected who open and deliver. Those who carry out executions — what scruples have they? How dare they behave so? Wounding the harmony of Heaven and Earth and damaging the blessing of body and household is worst in this matter of all. One cannot but take heed.

In the third year of the Wude era, Emperor Gaozu of the Tang decreed that in the first, fifth, and ninth months and on the ten fast days no executions should be carried out. The public regulations of earlier dynasties also forbade punishments and slaughter on the first of each month. To spare punishment on festival days is one expression of imperial benevolence. Do those who shepherd the people today ever embody it or not?

Dou Gui of the Tang, elder cousin of Empress Taimu, was commander of Luozhou. Stern and harsh, he was fond of killing and punished many of his officers and people. Whenever there was a case to decide, even in the months for covering bones and burying the dead, the time for emptying the prisons and loosing the fetters, he would not pause or spare. He also did away with the Minister Wei Yunqi. In the second year of the Zhenguan era he fell gravely ill. Suddenly he said that someone had come bringing melons. His attendants reported that there were none. Gui said: a whole plate of fine melons — how can you say there are none? Then he stared in alarm and said: these are not melons; they are human heads. They are coming with me to claim my life. He added: quickly, help me up; I must see Minister Wei. With those words he died. Carrying out executions on the eight nodes does not refer to killing alone; even flogging may not be done. Lenience and cruelty turn on a single thought, and calamity or auspiciousness then part as widely as cloud from mud. Those who hold office and those who manage a household should all take careful heed.

The stars and planets are in Heaven, passing through their palaces and circuits, and have nothing to do with man. Why spit at them? Foolish people recklessly declare them ominous and spit to ward them off. Talk of this kind truly comes from the empty tales of Qidong. But if the people lose their virtue, Heaven shows its changes; comets, eclipses, and meteors are in truth self-summoned. One should rather fear and cultivate self-examination, establish virtue to avert and atone. How can one spit at them? Duke Jing spoke three good words and the planet Mars withdrew from its station; the response to cultivated virtue is plain and no lie.

Red and white is called the hong; blue and white is called the ni. These are the qi of the union of yin and yang. The Book of Odes says: the rainbow is in the east; none dares point at it. The Spring and Autumn text Yun Dou Shu says: when stars scatter they become rainbows. One should know that the rainbow is truly the residual qi of the Dipper stars, made visible in form and color. Therefore when Confucius of old completed the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Classic of Filial Piety and announced it to the Northern Dipper, a red rainbow descended and became yellow jade with characters carved on it. Who then can say the rainbow is not the residual qi of the Dipper stars? If one points at it, how can one be without guilt?

The sun, moon, and stars are the three lights, also called the three chronograms. They are what Heaven spreads out to illuminate and observe below, and to hand down as models and laws. The Most High says: if you see the sun, the moon, the Northern Dipper, or the Southern Dipper, then solemnly knock your head and beg for their protection and for pardon of your transgressions; you must not treat them lightly and so invite calamity. The Daoist canon teaches men to sacrifice to the sun and moon: on the first day of the second month each year sacrifice to the sun, and on the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the moon, with incense, flowers, and vegetarian offerings, bowing and praying in order to repay their kindness and to cause men to gain blessing and lengthened years. Since this is so, may one point at or stare long at the sun, moon, and stars?

Zhou Hong said that in his district a crowd of people were drinking together when they saw an unusual light in the sun's disk at the edge of the sky. All together they pointed at it. Suddenly a violent wind and rain came up, and there fell a creature like a monkey with two eyes gleaming. The people fell to the ground in terror, and in a moment it was gone. The ears of all of them were stopped up with mud, and they were all afflicted with palpitations.

Cai Jing of the Song could stare at the sun for a long time without his eyes dimming. Some said this was a sign of nobility. Yet relying on the strength of his eyes he dared defy the sun, and those who understood knew he had a heart disloyal to his prince. In the end, because he monopolized power and ruined the state, he was exiled and died.

Sun Jin of the Yuan dynasty grieved and wasted away at his father's death; in harsh winter he walked barefoot. While the coffin lay unburied he never undid his belt. When he carried the coffin across the river, sky and earth grew dark; Jin prayed earnestly to the three lights, and the wind stopped and the waves stilled, and the sun showed itself for his sake. He was especially filial to his stepmother, née Tang. She once suffered from abscesses and Jin sucked them himself. Then she lost her sight, and Jin prayed to the three lights and licked her eyes, and her sight returned. Ten days after Tang died, as the burial approached, spring rains were falling bitterly; Jin wept at night, and the sky cleared, the clouds opened and the sun shone. When they reached the grave it was dusk and there was no light; Jin cried out in grief again, and the starlight blazed out, the moon out of season suddenly bright as day. Seen thus, the three lights above not only have the grace of shining upon us; they also answer as soon as prayed to. How can one trifle with them, point at them, and so bring on oneself grave guilt?

To burn the forest in hunting is called burning-hunt. Shooting the flying and chasing the running the Most High already forbids in plain terms; how much more the burning-hunt, whose slaughter is without limit? The reason spring is specified is that spring is the season of growth and generation, and to do such a thing then is to defy the course of Heaven above and to kill living beings below, a lack of benevolence most extreme. It is not that the other months need no heed.

Liu Moer of the Tang died on the same day as his son. A neighbor named Qi had died of illness and come back to life; he told how he had gone to the underworld and seen Moer and his son in a cauldron of boiling water, their skin and flesh all gone, only white bones visible; after a long while they took their original form again, then dissolved again, and again after a while re-formed, without any end. King Yama said: this man was devoted to hunting with fire, and so receives this retribution. All living beings share the Buddha-nature; how can one lightly kill them? Hunting is already wrong — how much more when it is done with fire? The myriad creatures are scorched and withered, the hundred hibernating things are burned to ashes; the harm is more than one can bear to speak of. The Monthly Ordinances of the Book of Rites are very detailed in their prohibitions, and the Most High takes it up again as a warning, because it concerns living life; hence his repeated orders and reiterated injunctions.

Spittle and mucus are but small matters, yet toward the north they are already a transgression; how much more abusive cursing? The foolish are driven by a heart of anger and have no leisure for scruples, never thinking: I wish to vent my rage — but what of the rage of the spirits?

Of the four verbal offenses of the world's people, abusive cursing is the worst. The scriptures say: the poison of ordinary men blazes, the fire of wrath ever burns; touched by circumstance they breed hatred, meeting a condition they raise obstructions. Therefore when a single angry word is spoken it rushes from the mouth and burns the heart, injuring the one before one with pain like a knife cut, wounding many, bringing measureless affliction. Even if living beings are without fault in body, if they are careless in verbal karma they too fall into evil paths.

A woman of Xin'an was fierce by nature and childless, and envied the son born to her husband's concubine. Every dusk she faced the north and cursed with foul words. One evening she cursed again, and suddenly saw a star fall to the earth, as large as a bushel, with a sound like thunder. The woman was so frightened that she fell ill, and her belly gradually swelled as if she were with child. When the time came for birth, for seven days nothing came; in truth there was nothing in her belly at all. She recovered only after repentance. The gleaming spirits are present everywhere; that the north alone is named is to stress that this direction is the gravest of all. Since this is so, should one not at all times remember that the ghosts and spirits are thickly arrayed about, and fear them and cultivate self-examination?

The Perfected One Ying Shi says: no living creature may be killed, and the turtle and the snake, being yin essences answering to the northern constellation of the Perfected Warrior, may especially not be killed. To kill them without cause will surely bring down miserable retribution. Therefore the benevolent ever earnestly protect and save them.

A villager of Yuezhou drained a pond to take fish, and because he caught many turtles he cut the flesh from them all and carried the shells to Jiangling to sell, making a rich profit. When he returned his whole body broke out in sores; he screamed in pain, and people could not bear to hear it. A great basin had to be filled with water and hands had to rub him before he was a little eased. Afterwards his skin fell away and his bones showed, and he turned into the form of a turtle and died with his flesh split and rotting.

Beside the house of a rich man stood a dead tree that he was about to cut down. He dreamed of a man leading a crowd to beg for a delay: wait until we have finished moving, then cut as you please. Waking, he sent a man up the tree to look, and saw snakes in it coiled and knotted without number. He at once ordered fire set to burn them. Before long, at midnight, flying fire was seen entering the rooms of his house; when they rose to fight it, all was still. This happened many times and they thought nothing strange of it. One evening a maidservant left fire in the firewood, and it spread into a prairie blaze; the family, taking it for the same old thing, slept on and did not rise, and when at last they tried to flee it was too late. The whole household was burned.

Liu Yanhui's father was prefect of Huzhou. A man came from the White Silver Pit and presented a great turtle, saying: whoever eats this turtle may live a thousand years. Yanhui's father secretly sent it back to where it came from. After his father died, Yanhui was an official of Fangzhou, when suddenly mountain floods came in fury and the flat ground was several feet under water. The whole household had no road of escape, when of a sudden a great turtle led the way, and every place it went was shallow. Thus they escaped the disaster. That night he dreamed of a man in white who said: I am the turtle of the White Silver Pit whom your father sent back. Therefore I have come to repay him.

Master Sun the Perfected One of the Tang was walking in the mountains when he saw villagers striking a green snake. He bought it and set it free. Before long a youth welcomed the Perfected One into a royal palace, where one in crimson robes came out and said: yesterday my little son met with calamity; happily the Master saved him, and so I sent my eldest boy to welcome you here and to express a little of my gratitude. He was led into the inner palace, where a consort came with a boy in green robes, knocked her head and bowed, and thanked him again and again. He was pressed to stay three days, with rare delicacies and fine food, silk and gauze, pearls and jade — nothing was lacking. The Perfected One declined it all and would accept nothing, taking away only the thirty immortal prescriptions of the Dragon Palace that the Most High had bestowed. With these he saved countless lives. The Thousand Ducat Prescriptions of today indeed owes something to those thirty prescriptions.

Such offenses as these — this is the sentence that sums up the preceding text. Offense means acting contrary to right, and the matters that follow. The words from the Director of Fate onward explain precisely how one receives retribution according to karma. The scriptures say: karma arises from the mind, and the mind is the agent of karma; karma draws the mind and it receives form, the mind follows karma and it manifests a realm — as the shadow follows the form, and so the crooked and the straight are distinguished; as the echo answers the sound, and so the great and the small differ. There is no discrepancy by a hair, no error in the response. As for the saying that the calamity reaches sons and grandsons, this too is spoken with the three ages in view. In sum, distant in children and grandchildren, near in one's own person — this is the retribution that is bright and unfailing. For when the world's people pile up evil and practice deceit, wounding the Most High's heart that loves life and defying the ancestors' intent to protect, they bring their descendants to hardship and cut off their ancestral sacrifices; and some then ascribe it to fate, some to inborn endowment. Alas, the great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life; for plants and trees, birds and fish, one cannot bear to see them extinguished — how much less for man, the most intelligent of the myriad things, can one bear to destroy his sons and grandsons? Therefore unless a man is utterly wicked his line is not cut off forever, but when the evil retribution is not exhausted it reaches his sons and grandsons; this too is the constant order of things.

Yang Su of the Sui urged the enthronement of Emperor Yang, to the peril of the Sui house, and his son Yang Xuangan was in the end exterminated by Emperor Yang. Li Ji urged the enthronement of Empress Wu, overturning the Tang mandate, and his grandson Li Jingye was likewise destroyed by Empress Wu. This is calamity reaching sons and grandsons. As the saying goes: as you began it, so you end it; the retribution that returns what you sent out cannot be denied. People today, judging only by what lies before their eyes, see a certain man doing evil and unharmed and say: Heaven has no eyes. They see a certain man doing evil and prospering and say: evil brings blessings. Now, piled-up goodness leaves a surplus of blessing and piled-up evil a surplus of calamity; the word surplus covers very much. Extending it beyond oneself gives the case of sons and grandsons — how could it mean repayment the same evening it is incurred? Yet the Most High loves life, and the surplus calamity reaching a man's sons and grandsons is also meant to punish evil and encourage good. If a filial son or compassionate grandson cultivates his mind and establishes his person, piling up goodness and accumulating merit to atone for the faults of those before him and to lighten the penalty on himself, then this is what the Most High deeply hopes for.

According to the Buddhist scriptures, the teaching of rebirth through cause and effect: first, the heaven path; second, the immortal path; third, the asura path; fourth, the human path; fifth, the animal path; sixth, the hungry ghost path; seventh, the hell path. The heavens, the immortals, and the asuras indeed belong to accumulated and compounded causes, while the four paths of humans and animals are still more the fixed retribution of karmic conditions. Therefore I have examined this in detail. As for the human path: the word jen means to bear; in circumstances both contrary and favorable one can bear all with peace. Because in the time of cause one rejoiced in mind after mind, practiced the five constants and the five precepts, and performed the middling grade of the ten good deeds, one receives this human body. The scriptures say: to be a man of wealth and honor, or a king, or an elder, comes from having honored and served the Three Jewels. To be a man of proper appearance, fair of complexion, foremost in beauty, comes from forbearance. To be a man of diligence, never slothful, delighting in merit, comes from diligence. To be a man of calm demeanor, whose words and deeds are careful and true, comes from meditative concentration. To be a man of talent and insight, who fathoms the deep Dharma, expounds wonderful meaning, and awakens the deluded, so that those who hear his words trust them as treasures, comes from wisdom. To have a clear and pure voice comes from singing in praise of the Three Jewels. To be a man clean and free of illness comes from a mind of compassion. To be a man full of fear, with a hoarse and broken voice, comes from the hells. To be a man dull and stupid, slothful and gluttonous, whose speech is unclear, who is timid and weak, who delights in the company of fools, and who is especially fond of darkness, comes from the animals. To be a man unclean comes from having been a pig. To be a man fierce and cruel comes from having been a snake or viper. To have no sense of honesty comes from having been a dog. To be stubborn and self-willed comes from having been a sheep. To love fine food and drink, to kill living creatures at will, and to have no compassion comes from having been a jackal, wolf, fox, or hawk. To be unable to be calm and to be unable to bear things comes from having been a monkey. It is also said: to be a man of tall stature comes from having respected others; to be short comes from having slighted others; to be ugly comes from having been fond of anger; to be born knowing nothing comes from not having studied and asked; to be dull and foolish comes from not having taught others; to be short-lived and sickly comes from having loved to kill; to have no means of livelihood and to suffer constant poverty comes from having loved to steal; to have no children comes from having violated another's wife; to have children who are lewd and disorderly comes from having violated another's unmarried daughter; to be widowed, orphaned, and alone comes from having treated one's sons and daughters cruelly; to be a man who goes hungry comes from having loved to eat alone; to be a man or maidservant comes from owing debts unpaid and from failing to reverence the Three Honored Ones; to be a man ugly and loathsome comes from having blocked the Buddha's lamps; to be born a water buffalo comes from having been an official cruel and harsh, mean to the common people; to be born a river deer comes from having frightened people; to be born among dragons comes from having loved to jest and play; for the body to break out in foul sores that treatment cannot cure comes from having flogged people; for people to be glad at the sight of one comes from having been glad at the sight of others; for people to be displeased at the sight of one comes from having been displeased at the sight of others; to be held in prison with fetters and shackles on the body comes from having caged and shut up living beings; to be a man with a split lip comes from having loved to fish; to be born in the land of naked people comes from having worn light clothing and burst in upon the Buddha's dwelling; to be born in the land of horse-hoof people comes from having worn shoes into the Buddha's ground; to be born in the land of pierced chests comes from giving alms and doing good and then regretting it. All such persons, having paid off their past debts in full, are again shaped into human form; but all of them, from beginningless time, have been turned upside down by karma, begetting one another and killing one another, and if they do not meet a Tathagata and do not hear the true Dharma, then within the toil of dust they revolve by the very law of things. Such as these are called pitiable ones. As for the animal path: their nature is dull and deluded and they cannot stand on their own, being raised by humans; hence they are called animals. Because in the time of cause they were deluded and greedy and performed the lowest grade of the ten evil deeds, they receive this body. The scriptures say: when the karma of ghosts is exhausted, one is then born into the world; meeting the person one wronged before, the two stand facing each other in enmity, and one becomes an animal to repay the old debt. Such things are all drawn forth by one's own false karma. If one awakens to bodhi, then this false condition is fundamentally nonexistent. As for the hungry ghost path: these ghosts are emaciated, ugly, and loathsome, ever coveting a single full meal, constantly suffering blows, filling rivers and blocking seas, enduring measureless suffering. Because in the time of cause they were miserly and greedy by nature and flattering and deceitful in mind, performing the middling grade of the ten evil deeds, they receive this body. The scriptures say: these living beings all fall by pure passion; the fire of karma dries them up and they come forth above as ghosts. Such things are all drawn forth by one's own deluded karma. If one awakens to bodhi, then wonderful realization is perfect and bright, and fundamentally there is nothing at all. As for the hell path: it means beneath the earth. But these hells differ in size and in the length or brevity of their spans. Those who suffer in them each have their own gravity and number of kalpas according to their deeds. The gravest of them die and are born ten thousand times in a single day, through measureless kalpas. Because in the time of cause their minds were thought after thought of greed, hatred, and delusion, creating the most evil karma, performing the highest grade of the ten evil deeds, they receive this body. The scriptures say: all these are deceived by living beings' own karma; they create the ten habitual causes and receive the six interwoven retributions.

First, the habit of lust, in intercourse, is aroused through mutual friction. Ground and rubbed without cease, it thus produces a great fierce fire that breaks out within, as when a man rubs his own hands together and the sensation of warmth appears. The two habits ignite each other, and so there come to be the iron bed, the copper pillar, and the like. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, describing the practice of lust, all name it the fire of desire. A bodhisattva seeing desire avoids it as he would a pit of fire. Second, the habit of greed, in scheming, is aroused through mutual suction. Drawing and grasping without cease, it thus produces accumulated cold and hard ice, frozen and bitter within, as when a man sucks in air through his mouth and a sensation of cold arises. The two habits press against each other, and so there come to be the sounds tsa-tsa and pa-pa, the blue, red, and white lotuses, the cold ice, and the like. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, describing much craving, all name it the water of greed. A bodhisattva seeing greed avoids it as he would a sea of plague. Third, the habit of pride, in mutual contempt, is aroused through reliance on self. Racing and flowing without cease, it thus produces soaring and rushing waves, and the gathered waves become water, as when the tongue and mouth savor themselves and moisture therefore arises. The two habits drum against each other, and so there come to be the river of blood, the river of ash, the hot sands, the sea of poison, the molten copper poured down the throat, and the like. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, describing self-conceit, name it drinking the water of delusion. A bodhisattva seeing pride avoids it as he would a great flood. Fourth, the habit of anger, in mutual clash, is aroused through opposition. Knotting and tangling without cease, the mind grows hot and gives forth fire, and the casting of qi becomes metal. Thus there come to be the mountain of knives, the iron pegs, the forest of swords, the wheel of swords, the axes and halberds, spears and saws, as when a man harbors a grudge and the killing breath flies and stirs. The two habits strike against each other, and so there come to be castration and beheading, hacking and stabbing, pounding and beating, and the like. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, describing hatred, name it sharp knives and swords. A bodhisattva seeing anger avoids it as he would execution. Fifth, the habit of deceit, in mutual enticement, is aroused through mutual mockery that is drawn out and cannot stop. Thus there come to be the rope and the wooden rack, as when water soaks a field and grass and trees grow. The two habits extend into each other, and so there come to be fetters, shackles, and chains, whips, staves, and clubs, and the like. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, describing treachery and falsehood, all name it the slanderous robber. A bodhisattva seeing deceit avoids it as he would a jackal or wolf. Sixth, the habit of fraud, in mutual cheating, is aroused through mutual deception. Deceiving without cease, the flying mind works villainy; thus there come to be dust and earth, dung and urine, filth and impurity, like dust before the wind, with nothing seen anywhere. The two habits add to each other, and so there come to be drowning and tossing, flying and falling, drifting and sinking, and the like. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, describing cheating and fraud, all name it robbery and murder. A bodhisattva seeing fraud avoids it as he would tread on a snake. Seventh, the habit of enmity, in mutual dislike, is aroused through cherished hatred. Thus there come to be the flying stones and hurled missiles, the box that stores and the cart that cages, the jar that holds and the sack that smothers, as when a man secretly poisons himself and nurses evil in his breast. The two habits devour each other, and so there come to be throwing and seizing, striking and shooting, casting and pinching, and the like. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, describing an enemy, name him the spirit of violation and harm. A bodhisattva seeing enmity avoids it as he would drink poisoned wine. Eighth, the habit of views, in mutual illumination, as with the satkaya view and the clinging to rites and precepts, the various karmas of erroneous understanding, is aroused through rejection and opposition, giving birth to mutual contradiction. Thus there come to be the king's envoys and presiding clerks, the records of testimony and attachment, as when travelers on the road meet one another coming and going. The two habits cross each other, and so there come to be examination and interrogation, weighing and trickery, trial and inquest, investigation and inspection, exposure and illumination, and the like. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, describing evil views, all name it the pit of views. A bodhisattva seeing all false and one-sided clinging is as though standing at a poisonous chasm. Ninth, the habit of injustice, in mutual addition, is aroused through false accusation. Thus there come to be the closing mountain and the closing stone, the crushing mill and the grinding grindstone, as when a slanderous robber oppresses the good and innocent. The two habits press against each other, and so there come to be pressing and pinning, pounding and weighing, squeezing and filtering, measuring and assessing, and the like. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, describing resentment and slander, all name it the slanderous tiger. A bodhisattva seeing injustice is as though struck by lightning. Tenth, the habit of litigation, in mutual proclamation, is aroused through concealment and covering. Thus there come to be the mirror and the candle that illuminate, as in broad daylight where no shadow can be hidden. The two habits set each other forth, and so there come to be evil friends, the mirror of karma, the fire pearl, the exposure of past karma, and the verification of accounts, and the like. The Tathagatas of the ten directions, describing concealment, all name it the hidden robber. A bodhisattva contemplating concealment is as though bearing a high mountain and treading the great sea. What are the six retributions? All living beings create karma through the six consciousnesses, and the evil retribution they draw forth comes out through the six faculties. First, the retribution of sight, drawing forth evil fruit. When this karma of sight is interwoven, then at the moment of death one first sees a fierce fire filling the ten directions, and the dead one's spirit-consciousness flies and falls, riding the smoke into the unintermitted hell. Second, the retribution of hearing, drawing forth evil fruit. When this karma of hearing is interwoven, then at the moment of death one first sees waves and billows drowning heaven and earth, and the dead one's spirit-consciousness pours down, riding the current into the unintermitted hell. Third, the retribution of smell, drawing forth evil fruit. When this karma of smell is interwoven, then at the moment of death one first sees poisonous vapor filling far and near, and the dead one's spirit-consciousness springs up from the ground into the unintermitted hell. Fourth, the retribution of taste, drawing forth evil fruit. When this karma of taste is interwoven, then at the moment of death one first sees the iron net and fierce flames blazing, covering the world around, and the dead one's spirit-consciousness passes down and hangs on the net, head hanging upside down, into the unintermitted hell. Fifth, the retribution of touch, drawing forth evil fruit. When this karma of touch is interwoven, then at the moment of death one first sees a great mountain closing in from four sides with no way out, and the dead one's spirit-consciousness sees a great iron city with fire snakes and fire dogs, tigers, wolves, and lions, and ox-headed jailers holding spears and lances, driving him through the city gate toward the unintermitted hell. Sixth, the retribution of thought, drawing forth evil fruit. When this karma of thought is interwoven, then at the moment of death one first sees an evil wind blowing down the land, and the dead one's spirit-consciousness is blown about, spinning and falling in the sky above, and riding the wind drops into the unintermitted hell. These are called the ten causes and six fruits of hell, all created by the delusion of living beings. Their various causes and effects are too many to set out in full. Here I take only those that bear closely on retribution through the three ages and append them, in order to make clear the principle of weighing, lightening, and remitting, so that the mirror of warning may be bright and men may know where to take alarm.

The preceding text has already made clear that retribution follows the deed; this section speaks again of taking by force, and it is addressed to those who have power. This one matter is the extreme of inhumanity and unrighteousness, and it is also what men find it hardest to avoid; therefore it is singled out once more to show them. Heng means violent and tyrannical; it is to overbear by force and threaten by power. Zhi means the original amount; to match the original amount is to equal exactly the sum originally taken. Now he who takes another's wealth by force mostly does so for the sake of wife, children, and household, not knowing that the Director of Fate is precisely reckoning up his wife, children, and household in order to repay his greedy evil, so that his gain serves only to ruin him. To exchange living flesh and blood for lifeless gold and silver is surely too pitiful. And when evil is piled up and the tally is spent, one's own person cannot escape death either; what use then is this gold and silver? If one wishes to bribe and work the channels of the underworld, I fear it will hardly be indulged. When that hour comes, who is there who will not see it all as emptiness? Only, it is a little late. Why not, before that hour comes, early put oneself in that position and think? If one is lucky and the evil is somewhat light, so as not to come to death, then water and fire, bandits and thieves, lost and ruined goods, sickness and quarrels, unworthy sons and grandsons — the roads by which my wealth is whittled away are very many. Now he who takes another's wealth by force, and the one in the darkness who holds the great abacus, also takes by force. In the end there is no money at all, and there are the terror of water and fire and bandits, the chagrin of goods lost, the agony of sickness, the resentment and humiliation of quarrels, the shame and stain of unworthy sons and grandsons. One has plainly suffered loss to no purpose and has no way to recover it; and one still owes how much in guilt, with no freedom, unable to pay it off. What is to be done, what is to be done? Let him who takes by force think on this: it will not only chill his heart; it should also ash it.

When Xing Shu was sent as envoy to Silla, on his way back he halted at Tanshan and saw more than a hundred merchants carrying several boatloads of goods worth several hundred thousand strings of cash. Shu attacked and killed them and took their goods. In time his son Xing Zai plotted rebellion with Wang Hong and was executed, and of his wife, children, and household not one survived. Wei Gonggan was prefect of Qiongzhou and took much by force; when his term ended and he returned, his boat capsized in the water and all his goods and wealth were lost, and he barely escaped with his life. Lu Shizao was prefect of Chizhou and preyed on the common people, returning home with a heavy load, when suddenly fire burned his goods, leaving the boat and the men entirely unharmed. Ding Wei was banished to Zhuyai and was robbed by bandits, losing everything, and died soon after. Ma Xiang was greedy by nature and served as transport commissioner of Sichuan; when the rebellion of Liu Xu came, Xiang put his gold down a well, and when the trouble was over he could not retrieve it, and all he had was gone. Hu Yinggui and Lu Yiqi together lured the son of an official family into gambling and took his family wealth; suddenly Hu went blind in one eye and Lu lame in one foot, and they ended their days crippled, poor, and destitute. Qiang Huairen was greedy and overbearing and grew very rich; his son was unworthy, devoted to gambling and whoring, and there was not a day without quarrels and lawsuits, and within ten years the family was emptied, and he ended down and out in bitter poverty, with his descendants unable to rise. All the above took the wealth of others by force and were shown retribution according to the deed, as cases answering to the exact amount. The gravest of them is the death and extinction of Xing Shu's person and household. There are unclear matters in the world, but Heaven has no unrewarded article. A man may be skillful in plotting, but Heaven is more skillful in retribution. Oh, how fearful.

The text above spoke of taking by force; that wrongful killing is spoken of next is because wrongful killing always arises from loving wealth and grudging to part with it. The meaning is the same as Mencius' saying that in such a case it is not the man himself who kills them, but the difference is only a hair. This is most direct and satisfying. Of wrongful killing let me set out the causes briefly; there are seven. First, judging cases: taking bribes and wronging the innocent, giving way to a cruel nature. Second, waging war: slaughtering and plundering for wealth, faking heads to claim merit. Third, using medicine: seeking profit and causing death by error, obscuring principle and attacking wrongly. Fourth, destroying pregnancy: grudging expense and drowning girl infants, giving way to lust and procuring abortion. Fifth, the worms of the yamen: cheating for wealth and entrapping others, deceiving superiors and being wantonly cruel. Sixth, geomancy: moving graves to harm others, choosing deadly sites and bringing disaster. Seventh, incompetent teachers: ruining a man for life, harming his sons and brothers. The killing differs, but the wrongful destruction is the same. Such offenses as these the law does not pardon; if no human calamity comes, a heavenly punishment must. Though it be called killing others, it is in truth only killing oneself.

A certain Chan master of the Song dynasty, when young, got drunk and fought with a man over money, and the man fell dead on the spot. Fearing punishment, he fled far away, left home, and practiced bitterly, and so attained thorough awakening and became a great Chan master, opening the hall and preaching to several hundred students. When he was over seventy, one day he suddenly bathed, ascended the seat, and said to the assembly: do not move and do not speak; watch this old monk settle a case from forty years ago. He sat until noon, when an officer of a garrison suddenly burst in and bent his bow to shoot. The master joined his palms and said: this old monk has waited for you a long time. The officer started and said: I do not know you, Reverend; the moment I saw you I wanted to kill you, and I do not understand why myself. The master said: a debt is paid with money, a fair exchange; only please strike, do not hesitate. Then he turned to the assembly and said: after I die, invite this layman, give him a meal, and see him home. A single angry word against him, or defiance of Heaven and the Way, and you are no disciple of mine. The officer grew more doubtful and pressed him hard for the explanation. The master said: you have lived two lives, and so you have forgotten; I have lived one life, and so I have not forgotten. Then he told him what had happened before. The officer, who had never learned to read, suddenly chanted aloud: Vengeance answered by vengeance, when will it end? Kalpa after kalpa entwined, is it by chance? Better to dissolve it with the master here; and now at once I go to the Western Heaven. With those words, bow and arrow in hand, he stood erect and passed away. The master came down from the seat, shaved his head for him and gave him a name, changed his clothes and laid him in the coffin, then crossed his legs and, taking leave of the assembly, also passed away. Now to kill a man forty years before and pay with one's life forty years after: the claim is slow, but the debt is one. It is fortunate that both were men of great capacity, so that on the road of enemies they met face to face, and the evil adversary in the end became a good karmic bond. The officer's death pressed the creditor, and he cultivated and realized the Way; the Chan master waited for the debt-collector and was freed, and was born in heaven. It is a supreme and wondrous affinity such as is rarely met in a thousand ages. Had he not truly attained the Way, or had the officer lacked capacity, the debt would certainly not have been left unclaimed. Thus it is clear that killing another is no different from killing oneself. The seven causes of wrongful killing set out above — let men take heed of them deed by deed. Never lend a fierce debt rashly.

This section again makes clear the harm of coveting profit, because the world's people weigh profit heavily in their hearts; hence the author does not shrink from repeating his words. The Most High's grandmotherly heart admonishes again and again, to the utmost. Among the offenses of the human world, such as lust, killing, and treason, the deeds are not easy to commit and the men are not often seen; but in the one path of taking wealth there are a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations, beyond all tracing. In the world there is no day on which wealth is not used, and therefore no man who does not take wealth. Since there is no man who does not take it, then in the taking, the righteous are few and the unrighteous many — no need to ask to know it. What is righteous? It is feeling and principle, that is all. If I take and the other gladly gives, that is called near to feeling and is called righteous. If he does not gladly give, then it is not near to feeling and not righteous. If I take and can tell others of it, that is called reasonable and is called righteous. If I cannot tell others, then it is unreasonable and not righteous, no matter whether the amount is great or small. If one could take what is not righteous and still use it in peace, then what harm would there be in following what suits men's hearts and letting them do as they please? But the Most High admonishes so earnestly because he knows that where there are men who take wealth unrighteously, there are men who lose wealth unrighteously. One man is pleased, one man is grieved; or one man is pleased and ten are grieved, a hundred are grieved, a thousand or ten thousand are grieved. The way of Heaven loves to return; why should it favor the pleased and slight the grieved? Then the grievance in the darkness, and those who would set the matter straight, will surely all roll up their sleeves and rise. The Most High knew the reason, and spoke plainly to warn men: do not take. Men did not follow. He spoke gently to make it clear: it cannot be held. Men did not believe. He spoke sharply to urge them: what is gained thereby is inauspicious. Men still grasped at the moment and had no leisure for distant care. Nothing served but to wake them, saying: gain and no gain are the same. Then perhaps men's greed would be a little checked. Hence the parables of the dripped meat and the poisoned wine. Dripped meat and poisoned wine kill the moment they enter the mouth. Yet no man, however mad and foolish, who knows a thing to be dripped meat or poisoned wine, will still gorge and drink and lift cup and chopsticks. If men knew that unrighteous wealth is dripped meat and poisoned wine, then though thousands and tens of thousands came into their hands, they would lift up the coins and not use them. Is this not gain and no gain being the same? Now wealth gained but unused is a worthless discarded thing in the world. To exhaust the arts of the mind and spend every device of scheming in order to seek a worthless discarded thing in the world — what is that for? Yet the fragrance of dripped meat equals that of minced meat, and the sweetness of poisoned wine is not below that of amrita. Men see the fragrance and sweetness and will again raise a hopeful thought: perhaps it is not really poisonous after all. Few will be those who do not fill their cups and chew. When at last it can neither be spat out nor swallowed down, when the bowels break and the skin splits and death comes on the heels of the moment, then they sigh that they did not see it sooner. It is no use. Vegetable soup and wheat gruel, village wine and mountain greens: they have no great savor in the mouth, yet one is gently tipsy and quietly filled, patting one's belly well content. How far apart are their bitterness and joy? The verifying cases are scattered through the text above, detailed and complete. They will not be appended here.

He draws out the word mind to show men the first stirring of good and evil, wishing them to know to be careful at the source. Consider the words perhaps and or: they carry the sense that what begins from good may enter into evil. This should be read alongside Mencius' chapter on rising at cockcrow. The Buddhist scriptures say: within the three realms there is no separate dharma; it is made by the one mind alone. Again: it can follow conditions and be defiled or pure, and it creates the ten dharma realms everywhere. The world and beyond the world are not outside the four holy and six ordinary dharma realms. These ten dharma realms have no self-nature of their own; they are all made by the one mind. Originally this mind, though called unchanging, in fact follows conditions; because it follows conditions, it is said to be able to create. Therefore the mind can make a buddha, the mind makes living beings, the mind makes heaven, the mind makes hell. To say the mind arises is to say a single thought sprouts. Though a single thought is subtle, it moves Heaven and Earth and reaches through to the ghosts and spirits. If a man can raise one good thought, that single thought alone is the spirit talisman that breaks hell, the sword of wisdom that cuts down all evil, the compassionate ship that crosses the sea of suffering, the bright lamp that lights the darkness. If he raises one evil thought, then the three evil paths appear before him and he sinks without rest. Therefore auspicious and inauspicious spirits come with the thought, with not the least waiting. The Ming master Hanshan Deqing said: the thought must be seen through at the point where it arises; before the thing arrives, do not raise it in vain. If one can cut off an evil thought with a single stroke when it arises, then the root of karma is dissolved on the spot, and where can the deluded thought settle? The first stirring of passing beyond the ordinary and entering the holy lies entirely here.

Long ago Yuan Zishi hated a man named Miao for betraying his kindness and at the fifth watch set out to kill him. On the way he passed a hermitage whose master, Xuanyuan Weng, was rising early to recite scriptures, and saw several hundred ghosts of strange and monstrous shapes following Yuan as he went, each holding knives and axes, their bearing most ferocious. After a short while they came back, and then the people accompanying him wore golden crowns and jade pendants, gathered in companies of a hundred or more, with incense, flowers, banners, and standards, and faces mild and joyful. The master called him in and asked, and Zishi told him: Miao betrayed my kindness, and I was going to kill him; but when I reached his gate I thought that though Miao has wronged me, what guilt have his wife and children? And he has an aged mother. To kill him alone is in truth to kill his whole family. How could my heart bear it? So I turned my thought and came back. The master told him what he had seen and congratulated him, saying: the spirits already know your deed; you will surely have generous emolument. Zishi then pressed forward bravely in goodness, ever increasing. In the end he passed the examinations and rose to the rank of minister. Laozi said: between good and evil, how far apart are they? I have often repeated these words. On the whole, the two roads of good and evil are not far apart at first; the difference lies only in the everyday point where a thought arises, whether it is so or not so. If one can know this principle and constantly and earnestly cultivate self-examination, then naturally the whole being will be good, blessing will unfailingly increase, and calamity will unfailingly retreat. Look at Master Yuan's one good thought turning calamity into blessing, and so swiftly. It is as said: when the mind raises good or evil, the auspicious and inauspicious spirits already follow it. The proof is here — is it not all the more surely to be believed?

This section draws out the two words change and repent, to show men the method of turning to good and correcting faults, and the pivot by which calamity is reversed into blessing. To change is to correct one's faults; to repent is to confess them. In the world the wholly good are few, while those who have done evil are many; yet the ungood can all become utterly good again. Therefore the Most High speaks with a bitter mouth and many words, and at the close of the book brings out the essential meaning of change and repentance, shouting down the barrier of delusion and bringing men back to the shore. But then he feared that men would misread the two sayings "put down the butcher's knife" and "become a buddha on the spot," and vainly think to save a cartload of burning firewood with a single cup of water. Therefore he says: commit no evil — hoping they will scrape and polish it all away. And again: practice every good — hoping they will accumulate it to fullness.
